analysis.one_liner: Lets Medicare negotiate drug prices, caps out-of-pocket drug costs, and opens drug imports from Canada.
analysis.headline: The Prescription Drug Affordability Act was introduced in September 2015 with one cosponsor, referred to the Senate Finance Committee, and never received a hearing, a vote, or further action before Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have required the government to negotiate prescription drug prices for people on Medicare, closed the Medicare coverage gap sooner, made drug makers pay rebates for drugs used by low-income patients, allowed personal importation of lower-priced drugs from Canada, restricted patent settlements that delay generic competition, and required manufacturers to disclose their costs, profits, and pricing. It was sent to the Senate Finance Committee the day it was introduced and stayed there for the rest of the two-year Congress.
analysis.who_benefits: Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries, especially the roughly tens of millions who hit the Part D coverage gap or get low-income subsidies, would pay less out of pocket. Patients generally would benefit from faster generic competition and the option to buy drugs from Canada at lower prices. Taxpayers would save on federal drug spending.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries and taxpayers

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Secretary of Health and Human Services to negotiate prices with pharmaceutical manufacturers for drugs covered under Medicare Part D, replacing the current 'noninterference' rule that bars such negotiation [S2][S3].
Accelerates the closing of the Medicare Part D coverage gap (the 'donut hole'), moving full closure from 2020 to 2017 and increasing the manufacturer rebate within the gap to 75 percent [S2][S3].
Requires drug manufacturers to pay rebates for drugs dispensed to low-income Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries, mirroring the rebates already required in Medicaid [S2][S3].
Extends Medicaid's additional rebate requirement to generic drugs, which had previously been exempt from the inflation-based rebate [S2][S3].
Allows individuals to import prescription drugs from Canada and potentially other countries, where prices are often lower [S2][S3].
Presumes 'pay-for-delay' patent settlements anticompetitive unless they fall within narrow exceptions, and lets the FTC enforce that presumption, which would speed generic drugs to market [S2][S3].
Terminates a drug maker's market exclusivity if it commits or fails to report a drug-related violation such as fraud, misbranding, or illegal marketing [S2][S3].
Requires manufacturers to publicly report annual data on research and development spending, manufacturing costs, marketing, profits, federal benefits received, and foreign sales prices [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers would bear the direct cost, through negotiated lower prices, larger rebates on drugs sold to low-income patients and in the coverage gap, the loss of pay-for-delay settlements, and the possible loss of exclusivity for violations. Generic manufacturers would lose some Medicaid rebate shelter. Plan sponsors would face new reporting duties.

drawbacks.text: Direct government price negotiation could give the Secretary sweeping leverage to set prices, and opponents argued this would reduce manufacturers' revenue available for research and development, potentially slowing the introduction of new medicines [S2][S3].

Drug importation has faced safety objections: the FDA has historically warned it cannot guarantee the safety of drugs bought abroad, and critics note that countries like Canada have limited supply capacity if US consumers buy in bulk (general policy knowledge, not covered in the provided sources).

Allowing manufacturers to lose market exclusivity for violations could create large penalties layered on existing fraud enforcement, and critics would argue that may push some drugs out of the market or discourage companies from bringing products to the US (general policy reasoning).

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core of the bill is a transfer of billions in prescription drug costs from Medicare and Medicaid beneficiaries and taxpayers to brand-name drug manufacturers, achieved through the same tools the government already uses in Medicaid (negotiated rebates) and in other countries (price negotiation). The safety and innovation objections are the standard arguments raised against every drug-pricing bill and were not tested here because the bill never advanced. Its main design risk is that many provisions depend on aggressive administrative implementation by HHS.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in September 2015, read twice, and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, where it stayed until Congress ended in January 2017; it never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote.

narrative.text: Senator Bernie Sanders introduced the bill on September 10, 2015, joined by one cosponsor, Senator Al Franken (D-MN) [S1][S4].
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance [S5].
The action history shows no further activity — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action — before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017 [S5].
The bill had only one cosponsor from among 44 Senate Democrats and no Republican support, so it never had the coalition needed to move through a committee controlled by the majority [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers benefit from the outcome: none of the negotiation, rebate, importation, or pay-for-delay provisions ever took effect, so their pricing power in Medicare, Medicaid, and the retail market was untouched. Patients on Medicare continued paying the existing out-of-pocket schedule, and the coverage gap closed on the pre-existing ACA timeline rather than the accelerated one this bill would have set.

for.name: Sen. Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Prescription Drug Affordability Act of 2015 on September 10, 2015 and referred it to the Senate Finance Committee.

for.name: Sen. Al Franken
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; the only cosponsor recorded.

against.name: Senate Finance Committee (114th Congress)
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by a Republican majority
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — leaving it to die at the end of the Congress.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: Held the Senate majority and chaired the Finance Committee during the bill's two-year pendency; none cosponsored and no action was scheduled on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: The bill's support was an independent and a single Democrat against a 54-seat Republican majority that controlled the Finance Committee and scheduled nothing; no Republican cosponsored it [S4].

industries.note: The bill would impose negotiated Medicare prices, expanded rebates for low-income patients and in the coverage gap, a ban on pay-for-delay settlements, disclosure of costs and profits, and possible loss of market exclusivity for fraud violations. Its death left the industry's Medicare pricing and patent-settlement practices unchanged.

Pay-for-delay restrictions would end the practice of brand-name firms paying generics to stay off the market, which generic makers support, but the bill would extend Medicaid's inflation-based additional rebate to generic drugs, raising their rebate liability.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and Medicare Part D plan sponsors (PDP and MA-PD plans)
industries.note: Plans would be required to report per-drug pricing and rebate data and face civil penalties up to $10,000 per day for late or false reporting, while negotiated lower prices could reduce their drug cost exposure.

The bill would have allowed pharmacists, wholesalers, and individuals to import drugs from Canada, opening a new cross-border sales channel — with safety-regulation obligations on the Secretary to issue rules first.
